lead: A hard question reaches the young Church: must Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses in order to be saved? Antioch does not settle it alone. It sends Paul and Barnabas up to Jerusalem, to the apostles and the elders. The Gospel repeats Sunday’s passage of the vine and the branches, and today it is heard beside a Church learning how to stay one. Psalm 122 is a pilgrim song of going up to Jerusalem, the city built to be bound firmly together. Today the Church also remembers St Peter Chanel, martyr, and St Louis Grignion de Montfort, priest.

set: Since Peter baptised the Roman centurion Cornelius and his household (chapters 10–11), Gentiles had been entering the Church. At Antioch Jews and Gentiles believed and ate together. Now some believers from Judea teach that Gentiles must first be circumcised. The apostles’ letter will later say that these men had no instructions from them (15:24).

The question was not foolish. Circumcision was the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:10–14), and the Law was Israel’s treasured gift. The believers from the party of the Pharisees (v. 5) were taking God’s covenant seriously; Paul himself had been a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). Many scholars connect this meeting with the visit to Jerusalem Paul describes in Galatians 2:1–10, while others think that was an earlier visit. It is usually dated around AD 49.
str: vv. 1–2: teachers from Judea at Antioch; sharp debate; Paul and Barnabas are sent to Jerusalem.
v. 3: on the way through Phoenicia and Samaria they bring great joy.
vv. 4–5: welcome in Jerusalem; some believers from the Pharisees insist on circumcision.
v. 6: the apostles and the elders meet.
kw: The covenant sign given to Abraham. The question was whether Gentiles who believed in Israel’s Messiah had to become Jews first.
Leaders of the Jerusalem church who now appear beside the apostles (11:30). The word gives us the English “priest” through the Latin presbyter.
Literally a matter to be searched out. The Church does not pretend the question is easy; she gathers to seek the answer together.
vv: Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.
The issue is not a custom but salvation itself. That is why it could not be left to each local church.
Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them,
Luke does not hide that the first Christians quarrelled. What matters is what they did with the quarrel: they took it to the apostles.
they reported the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the believers.
On the road to a difficult meeting they tell good news. The joy of the believers in Phoenicia and Samaria is already part of the answer.
The apostles and the elders met together to consider this matter.
A Church that listens, debates and decides together under the apostles. The pattern of every later council is here.
ch: The Church has long seen in this assembly at Jerusalem the pattern of her councils: the bishops, with Peter, gather, listen to what God has done, consider the Scriptures, and decide. The disagreement was real and was not resolved by one side shouting louder, but by coming together in the Spirit. Disputes in parishes and families can learn from this road: neither silence nor division, but going up together to seek the truth.

set: The passage was read on Sunday; today the weekday Lectionary reaches it in its course through John. Heard after the first reading, it has a fresh note. The branches at Antioch and Jerusalem were very different, Jew and Gentile, and yet there is one vine. Unity does not come from making all branches alike but from all abiding in Christ.
str: vv. 1–3: Christ the vine, the Father the vinegrower, the word that cleanses.
vv. 7–8: his words abiding in us, and the Father glorified.
kw: One who works the earth. The Father does not stand at a distance; he labours patiently over the vine.
The disciples are cleansed “by the word” (v. 3), and his “words” are to abide in them (v. 7). Abiding in Christ includes keeping his words in the heart.
In John the Father is glorified in the Son’s Passion and resurrection (13:31–32). Here he is glorified also in the fruit of the disciples.
vv: You have already been cleansed by the word that I have spoken to you.
Said after the washing of the feet (13:10). Every time we listen to his word with faith, the vinegrower is at work in us.
If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask for whatever you wish,
This is not a blank cheque. One whose heart is filled with his words learns to ask for what Christ wants, and such prayer is heard.
My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.
The Father’s glory is not taken from us. It shines when we become fully alive as disciples.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of the Holy Spirit in the liturgy, says that the Spirit is like the sap of the Father’s vine which bears fruit on its branches (CCC 1108). At the Jerusalem assembly the same Spirit kept the branches on the one vine, and at every Mass he gathers into one body people of every origin.

rite: St Peter Chanel was a French priest of the Society of Mary (the Marists) who went as a missionary to the island of Futuna in the Pacific. He was killed there on 28 April 1841, the first martyr of Oceania, and soon after his death the island became Christian. St Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort (died 28 April 1716) was a French priest who preached parish missions among the poor and wrote True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin, teaching that we go to Jesus through Mary. Both are optional memorials in the Roman calendar. Each in his own way abided in the vine and bore fruit beyond his own lifetime.
study: When there is disagreement in my family or parish, do I go silent, walk away, or seek the truth together with others?
What is one word of Jesus I want to abide in me this week?
